newsitem.title: USA: College dean among those mulled for Fed - sources.
newsitem.headline: College dean among those mulled for Fed - sources.

text.p: A college dean who headed an advisory council on Social Security is among those being considered by the Clinton administration for nomination to the Federal Reserve, government sources said on Wednesday.

Edward Gramlich, Dean of the School of Public Policy at the University of Michigan, was described as a top-flight economist whose research has ranged from poverty and income distribution to the economics of major league baseball.
Other candidates being considered, according to the sources, include former Office of the Comptroller senior official Douglas Harris.
An African American, Harris is an expert on derivatives and is currently an adviser at Bank of New York.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Wednesday that the administration was close to selecting its candidates for the two empty positions on the central bank board. The Senate must approve those choices.
"I think we are quite close to having a decision and I hope we will have an announcement fairly soon," Rubin told reporters in New York.

The two Fed posts opened up earlier this year with the departure of Janet Yellen for the White House's Council of Economic Advisers and Lawrence Lindsey for the conservative American Enterprise Institute think tank.

Government sources said that earlier reports that senior Fed official Ted Truman was being seriously considered for the job were not true. Truman is director of the international division at the Fed board.

Another rumored candidate, Christina Romer, a professor of economics at the University of California, has reportedly taken herself out of the running for personal reasons, sources close to the administration said.

Gramlich, a former acting head of the Congressional Budget Office, found himself back in the public spotlight in January when the government advisory council he chaired released its report on ways to shore up the Social Security pension system.

The council was split over how to do that, although all 13 members saw investments in equities as one way to help plug the system's future financing gap. The Social Security trust fund currently can only invest in Treasury debt.
